text:
The chair appeared on the curb sometime between Tuesday's trash pickup and Thursday, and I noticed it because I notice things—that has always been my particular affliction. It was a kitchen chair, or had been once, before the fire. The seat was intact, upholstered in vinyl the color of old mustard, but the backrest had burned down to a blackened ribcage of wood, and the whole thing leaned against a recycling bin as though it had walked there on its own and needed a rest. I passed it twice that morning, and both times I had the peculiar sensation that it was facing me.

I should explain that I'd been out of work for four months. This is relevant only because it accounts for the hours, the long loose hours that stretched around me like floodplain. I walked a great deal. I had routes. And it was on the Thursday route, the long one past the canal, that I first saw them.

They were standing at the corner of Degraw and Nevins, waiting for the light. He was tall and narrow, with a canvas jacket gone soft at the elbows. She was small, dark-haired, holding a paper grocery bag against her hip the way women hold infants. What stopped me was their stillness. Everyone else at that corner was in motion, checking phones, shifting weight. These two simply stood, side by side, not touching, with the settled patience of trees. When the light changed they crossed in unison, and I found myself crossing behind them.

I told myself I was going the same way. For the first two blocks I could almost believe it. But when they turned, I turned. When they paused so the man could retie his shoe, I paused too, affecting great interest in the window of a shuttered laundromat. The woman waited without impatience, her eyes resting on some middle distance, and I saw that something in her face kept refusing to settle. She had the look of a photograph developing, features arriving slowly out of gray.

It began to rain, lightly at first, then with committed seriousness, and still I followed. They walked perhaps eight more blocks, into a neighborhood where the row houses sat lower against the sky and the streets had an end-of-the-map quality. The gutters were already running brown.

They stopped at a narrow brick house, no different from its neighbors except that its stoop was painted a bright, almost defiant blue, and the man climbed the three steps and opened the door without a key. They went inside. A light came on in the front window, warm and ordinary.

And I stayed.

I told myself I was waiting out the rain. There was an awning across the street, the remnant of a closed bodega, and I stood under it as the water rose. The rain came down in ropes. The intersection flooded ankle-deep, then shin-deep, the water carrying leaves and plastic and, at one point, an entire potted geranium, sailing serenely past like a boat at a regatta. And through all of it I watched the lit window, and what I saw there was so unremarkable that it became, by degrees, the most remarkable thing I'd ever seen.

They were making dinner. That was all. He moved back and forth past the window with pans and plates; she sat at a table, tearing lettuce with her hands, slowly, leaf by leaf. They did not appear to speak. Once, he came and stood behind her chair and put his hand on her shoulder, and she did not look up, and he did not seem to expect her to. It was the tenderness of people tending something that has already finished happening, the way you might water a plant you know to be dead.

The water kept rising. It climbed the bottom step of their stoop, then the second, and it occurred to me that I should knock, should say something—though what? The rain had thinned to a drizzle, but the flood had its own logic now, the storm drains returning everything we'd given them.

Then she stood up.

She came to the window and looked out, directly across the street, and I understood with a cold drop in my stomach that she was looking at me—or through me, or at the thing the water was delivering to her door. Because I turned, following her gaze, and saw it floating there, turning slowly in the current that eddied against the stoop: the chair. The burned chair from my corner, four blocks and a whole drowned afternoon away, its blackened ribs to the sky, its mustard seat sloshing with rain. It had come home, or it had come to collect someone. It knocked gently against the second step, once, twice, like a visitor patient enough to be let in.

I looked back at the window. She was still there, and now he stood behind her, his hand again on her shoulder, and they watched the chair together with that same terrible composure, as if they had been expecting it for years. And I saw her face clearly for the first time, lit from below by the strange reflection of water, and I understood what had refused to settle in it all day: she looked like something that had been through a fire. Not burned—no scars, nothing so literal—but passed through, the way the chair had been passed through, ruined in one part and untouched in another. Some conflagration I couldn't see had taken half of her and left the rest standing, leaning against things, waiting at curbs.

He reached past her and drew the curtain. The window went warm and blank.

I stood there a while longer. The water had reached the top step; it would go into the house soon, and I found I believed they would let it, that they would sit at their table eating torn lettuce while it rose around their ankles, that the chair would come in on the flood and take its place at the table, and there would be three settings, or had always been.

The walk home took twice as long as it should have. The flood was receding, leaving its tidemark of leaves and grit on every stoop, and the streets smelled of drains. When I reached my corner I stood where the chair had been, though of course it wasn't there, and I understood that it had never been there at all, not really—that some things only pass through the visible world, carried on currents we don't perceive, from the places where they burned to the places where they're expected.

I went inside. I made dinner. I ate standing up at the counter, and I did not, for a long time, sit in any chair.
